attribution.note: Marcus's own concluding line in his post, stated in his own voice.

semantics.note: Faithful paraphrase. It describes the current state of adoption and of people's verdicts on it. Nothing is hedged, and no conditions were dropped.

contract.note: He left 'people' undefined. The contract reads the claim against the business survey he cited and uses national data as a check. That is an ordinary reading. 'Not ignoring' is read as broad, fast uptake, not universal use, which is fair to his words.

evidence.note: CNBC TEC, Oct 2024: a third of firms were still testing Copilot, which fits 'waiting to see'.
Half of respondents said it was too soon to judge Copilot's value. This directly matches the waiting-to-see part.
St. Louis Fed, Aug 2024: national adoption was faster than for PCs or the internet, so generative AI was not being ignored.
About 40% of US adults aged 18-64 used it, so most did not. This limits how far the claim reaches into the general public but does not meet the contradiction condition of little uptake.

reviews.rationale: Late-2024 surveys show fast, broad uptake: 79% of surveyed firms were using Copilot, and national adoption outpaced PCs and the internet. Half of the tech leaders said it was too soon to judge Copilot's value, and a third were still testing it. That meets the support condition. Most of the public had not used it (e4), but that weakens how far the claim extends; it is not a contradiction under a reading that 'not ignoring' means broad uptake.

attribution.note: Marcus reports his own reply and endorses it in the post.

semantics.note: Faithful. The claim has two parts: near-universal trial of AI, and incomplete satisfaction with it. Neither part is hedged.

contract.note: He named no population. The contract assesses both the general public and businesses, which is fair because he later says the business poll bears out his reply. Reading 'practically everyone' as close to all is the ordinary meaning. The outcome depends on which population is meant.

evidence.note: A nationally representative survey from Aug 2024 found about 40% of US adults aged 18-64 had used generative AI. That is far from 'practically everyone' for the public.
Only a quarter said Copilot was worth the cost. That supports 'not always satisfied'.
79% of surveyed tech leaders said their company used Copilot. That supports near-universal use under the business reading, though it measures company use, not personal trial.

reviews.rationale: The 'not always satisfied' part holds: only 25% said Copilot was worth it. The 'practically everyone has tried it' part holds for the surveyed business population, where 79% of firms used Copilot. It fails for the general US public, where only about 40% had used generative AI in Aug 2024. Because the result depends on a population he never named, the outcome is mixed.

That shows the surveyed population was not ignoring AI, as the support condition requires. Marcus's 'tried' is a close paraphrase of 'company is using it'.
